t: Twelve walled cities have been excavated, five of them large: Beikthano, Maingmaw, Binnaka, Halin and Sri Ksetra, the last more than 13 km round and larger than Pagan or Mandalay; three have been World Heritage Sites since 2014.
The Pyu were the first in Southeast Asia to adapt Brahmic script to a tonal language, and their calendar, begun at Sri Ksetra on 22 March 638, became the Burmese calendar still used in Myanmar.

Nanzhao's raids from 754 culminated in 832, when its warriors overran the Pyu country and carried off 3,000 prisoners from Halin; the Burmans then took over the Pyu realm, and by the 13th century the Pyu had become Burmans.
dyk: Tang records describe the Pyu as a humane people to whom war was virtually unknown, who wore silk cotton rather than silk so as not to kill silkworms, and whose boys entered the monastery from the age of seven until twenty.
ev: Tibeto-Burman-speaking Pyu enter the Irrawaddy valley from Yunnan by the Taping and Shweli rivers and settle the plains around the Irrawaddy–Chindwin confluence.
Halin's wooden city gates, its earliest dated artefacts, are made; the city in the Mu valley grows into the largest Pyu centre.
The Pyu adopt the Sakra Era, two years after it came into use in India.
On 22 March the Vikrama dynasty at Sri Ksetra launches a new calendar, which later becomes the Burmese calendar.
On 25 March King Duttabaung founds Sri Ksetra's second dynasty.
Sri Ksetra's embassy, with 35 musicians singing in Sanskrit, reaches the Tang court.
Nanzhao warriors overrun the Pyu country and take 3,000 prisoners from Halin.
The main walls of Pagan are built; the Burmans have taken over the Pyu realm and found the Pagan Empire in the mid-11th century.

f.capital: No single capital: Halin was the largest city until the 7th or 8th century, then Sri Ksetra near Prome (Pyay); Beikthano, Maingmaw and Binnaka were the other great cities
f.predecessor: Bronze and Iron Age rice-growing settlements of the Samon valley south of Mandalay, trading with China from 500 BCE
f.successor: The Pagan Kingdom of the Burmans, founded by the chronicles in 849 and unified under Anawrahta in the mid-11th century
